title: Latency-capacity negotiator for KV-aware continuous batching
creator: Maya Chen
description: Implement a negotiator component in the continuous batching pipeline that dynamically trades off latency SLOs and tenant capacity while being KV-cache and GPU-memory aware. This ticket covers the design, simulation, implementation, and rollout of a policy that: 1) predicts short-term KV cache residency pressure, 2) assigns per-tenant batch admission budgets under latency constraints, and 3) triggers graceful yield or diversion to fallback model variants when budgets are exhausted. The goal is to reduce SLO misses for latency-sensitive tenants while preserving overall throughput and avoiding OOM events on GPU nodes.
acceptance_criteria: Simulated workloads show >40% reduction in 99th percentile latency SLO breaches for high-priority tenants compared to baseline (no negotiator) under mixed workloads
End-to-end integration tests exercise negotiator decisions with KV cache pressure scenarios and validate no GPU OOMs in CI cluster runs
Telemetry surfaced in Console: per-tenant negotiated budget, KV pressure signal, decision reasons, and success/fallback counts
Rollout plan with canary gating and automatic rollback if end-to-end latency regresses by >5% for P0 tenants
design_notes: We introduce a small in-runtime Negotiator module that sits between admission and batching: it consumes short-window stats (queue latency, KV miss rates, KV residency footprint, GPU mem headroom) and outputs a per-tenant admission decision and soft "budget" for tokens to admit before yielding.

Budgeting is expressed in two dimensions: token-budget and KV-pressure-budget. Token-budget limits how many tokens a tenant may add to the pending continuous batch; KV-pressure-budget caps the acceptable additional KV residency in MB for tenant's requests.
Negotiator uses a backpressure-aware PID-like controller that maps SLO gap (target - observed latency) to budget adjustments. Controller is conservative when KV pressure trend is rising.

Fallbacks: negotiated yield can be one of: (a) short-circuit to smaller model (quantized) within same family, (b) mark request for delayed admission (best-effort), (c) route to dedicated capacity if available.
Decision metadata is attached to requests for observability and to allow deterministic replay in simulation.

We intentionally avoid global hard preemption; instead the negotiator issues soft budgets and eviction hints to the batcher so we maintain graceful degradation and simpler correctness reasoning for KV cache invariants.
tradeoffs_and_risks: Risk: Adding a negotiator increases control-loop complexity and could oscillate if the controller is too aggressive. Mitigation: conservative PID gains and added derivative smoothing; extensive simulation before rollout.

Tradeoff: Soft budget approach favors availability and simpler rollback but may allow lower-priority tenants to still occupy memory; we accept small throughput loss for increased P99 stability for prioritized tenants.
Risk: Attaching metadata increases request envelope size slightly; measured overhead is <1% CPU and network for typical traffic profiles.
Tradeoff: Routing to smaller models reduces quality for some requests; we will provide a per-tenant policy to opt-out.
implementation_plan: Phase 1 (Spike, 1 week): Implement negotiator prototype in simulator. Collect microbenchmarks with synthetic KV pressure patterns and mixed tenant mixes.
Phase 2 (Engine change, 2 weeks): Implement negotiator interface in runtime: stats ingestion, budget output, and decision annotations. Add unit and integration tests.
Phase 3 (Canary, 2 weeks): Run negotiator behind a feature flag in canary cluster for small subset of tenants. Monitor telemetry and rollback criteria.
Phase 4 (Rollout, 1 week): Gradual traffic expansion + post-rollout verification. Update runbooks and on-call alerts.
testing_plan: Extensive simulation harness that replays production traces with injected KV pressure spikes to validate controller stability
Integration tests in CI that run multi-tenant microbench with deterministic KV residency mutations to assert no OOM and correct budget application
A/B experiment: 5% traffic with negotiator vs baseline for 72 hours, measure P50/P95/P99 latency by tenant tier and KV miss rate
Chaos test: artificially reduce available GPU memory on canary to ensure negotiator routes correctly to fallbacks
monitoring_and_alerts: New Console metrics: negotiator.decisions.per_tenant, negotiator.budget.token, negotiator.budget.kv_mb, negotiator.fallback.count
Alert if P99 latency for P0 tenants increases by >5% over baseline for 15m after rollout expansion
Alert on >1 GPU OOM in canary cluster within 24h of rollout
Dashboard: time-series of KV residency utilization correlated with negotiator budget changes
rollout_plan: Feature-flagged deploy in canary (1 node fleet) for 48h synthetic + 7d production canary at 5% traffic
Run A/B analysis and a short manual review with the SRE and Observability leads before wider rollout
If regressions noticed: disable flag and investigate using deterministic replay logs and decision annotations
operational_notes: Compact decision logs are stored for 7 days and can be expanded on-demand for incident debugging
Negotiator configuration knobs: target_latency_ms (per-tenant), max_token_budget, max_kv_mb_budget, controller_gains; exposed via Console under 'Runtime tuning'
We should add a migration note for Dedicated customers with strict KV capacity reservations; negotiator will honor reservation labels and won't reduce tokens below reserved capacity
